My previous note appears to have been misconstrued, so let me add a brief clarification. As I always remind everyone, I am Forbes' "Worst Hedge Fund PM on Earth"—no need to take everything so seriously.

Too many ppl blaming this selloff on the wrong things. "Fed tightening" or "valuations"... are you out of your minds? My core point is that the underlying signs of market deterioration have been building steadily since June, just as Ace and Paulo have consistently highlighted. 

Everyone is familiar with the meme of the Reaper knocking sequentially on the doors of rates, precious metals, equity L/S, and macro.

Many attribute this move to Fed tightening, yet comparing pre- and post-selloff levels shows no meaningful shift in US FCI or Fed rate pricing. Financial plumbing and front-end funding markets also remain orderly. Perhaps someone could clarify what tightening is actually taking place.

I understand the widespread desire for a Fed pivot. Certainly the Fed would have been better served heeding voices like Danny Dayan rather than remaining passive when hawkishness was warranted. Whether a December hike is appropriate remains unclear—it likely leans toward a policy mistake.

Even so, that does not justify the pivot the market is hoping for. While the appetite for a post-pivot equity rally is understandable, there is simply no catalyst to warrant it—certainly not an equity market that has barely slipped into negative territory YTD.

Liquidity remains adequate, bank reserves are not under stress, and the Treasury market is functioning without dislocation. Meanwhile inflation remains well above target; having heard assurances for two years that it will eventually subside, I prefer to treat that trajectory as uncertain.

With long end yields having only recently stabilized, an unjustified pivot risks reigniting instability at the back end of the curve. Consequently, the Fed requires a clear pretext.

Current conditions fall short of providing one. Something must break. For now, asset prices have corrected without systemic stress—so unless market participants break something, the Fed lacks its excuse.

I do agree numerous assets look undervalued, especially non-AI and non-semi names caught in the crossfire. For long term investors accustomed to holding core positions patiently over multi-year horizons, accumulating here makes complete sense.

From a trader or PM standpoint, however anchoring a thesis on an imminent Fed pivot or compressed multiples is fundamentally flawed.

A pivot may materialize, but only after something breaks—and valuations were stretched to begin with. Low-quality companies were already trading at 50x to 100x earnings and continued to rally regardless.

It was not valuation itself halted that advance, but a broader shift in market dynamics. Equities ultimately declined at the tail end of a sequential deleveraging across quant, hedge fund books (Equity L/S and Rates RV), macro (precious metals and oil), dispersion, and EM FX.

Accordingly from a trading perspective, I want to see stabilization in the forces that initiated this tape: moderating correlations, the completion of cross-asset liquidations, and genuine liquidity returning via high vol accumulation candles—especially after this week's severely impaired equity liquidity.

That is all. I have no interest in buying in anticipation of a Fed pivot; if something must break first, the logical approach is to wait for that break before stepping in.

Long term investors should disregard all of this and simply buy—specifically sound, real-world businesses outside the AI and semi baskets that merely suffered collateral damage from financial deleveraging.

Investors need not think like traders; simply scale in gradually and let the results play out over the coming years. Gonna start adding some common stocks—including a few miners—to my LT portfolio soon too.

Last, i know folks who got wiped out on levered AI/semi bets are now chasing even worse junk stocks for a quick bailout.

It's your money sure—but losing your savings is recoverable; you can still live a full life.

Revenge-trading to make it back can permanently ruin your life and leave you buried in crippling debt. Thanks. Pushback always welcome—just keep in mind I have an 80 IQ. Enjoy the rest of your weekend guys.

Commodities: Speculative selling extends into a tenth week as metals bear the brunt

The latest COT report, covering managed money positioning across key commodity futures in the week to Tuesday, 17 November, showed continued risk reduction across most sectors, particularly metals, ahead of a brutal end to the week.

The combination of a dash for cash, dollar strength, rising US rate expectations and growing concerns about the AI investment boom was already weighing heavily on precious and industrial metals. Selling pressure accelerated sharply after Tuesday's reporting cut-off, suggesting the latest positioning data may understate the extent of the subsequent liquidation.

Overall, while the Bloomberg Commodity Index suffered a relatively modest 1% decline during the reporting week, before tumbling in the days that followed, the combined net long across the 25 major commodity futures tracked in this report fell for a tenth consecutive week, albeit at a much slower pace than in previous weeks. The aggregate net long declined by 32,377 contracts to 474,100, with selling once again concentrated in energy and, increasingly, metals.

The combined net long across 25 major commodity futures declined by 32k contracts to 474k, with selling slowing compared with previous weeks.

Metals bore the brunt:
Gold net long -9% to 104k contracts, a five-month low.
Silver's remaining net long virtually wiped out, leaving just 17 contracts.
Copper net long -21% to 27k, a 14-month low, down from 82k in September.

Energy: Combined Brent and WTI longs fell by 10k contracts to 203k amid growing concerns about a 2027 supply surplus. Gasoline longs fell 8%, while moderate short covering reduced the substantial natural gas net short by 5%.

Agriculture: Aggressive grain selling finally slowed, leaving the combined net long across six contracts at just 15k, down from around one million two months ago. Corn and both wheat contracts remain net short.

Softs: Cocoa and coffee attracted limited speculative buying despite strong price gains, while sugar and cotton saw further long liquidation.

The subsequent collapse in AI-related equities, stronger dollar, rising funding costs and broader dash for cash point to further liquidation that may become visible in next week's report.

The silver lining? Ten consecutive weeks of selling have substantially reduced speculative exposure, potentially laying the groundwork for a recovery once dollar liquidity pressures ease and attention returns to underlying supply constraints and supportive fundamentals.

More in my Monday update.

COT on #Forex: Dollar longs rise as speculators turn increasingly defensive

The latest IMM positioning data covers the week to Tuesday, 17 November, just ahead of one of the sharpest two-day US equity selloffs in years, driven by a collapse in the AI trade. By Friday, the Nasdaq Composite had shed more than USD 4 trillion in market value for the week, wiping out its entire year-to-date gain, while the Bloomberg Dollar Index closed at a 19-month high.

Even before the equity rout gathered momentum, speculators had already resumed buying dollars, albeit at a moderate pace, against nearly all currencies covered in this update. The notable exceptions were CHF, MXN and, somewhat surprisingly, sterling.

By Tuesday's close, the aggregate speculative dollar net long against eight IMM currency futures had risen 13% to USD 32.6 billion, still well below last month's peak above USD 43 billion and the multi-year high exceeding USD 50 billion reached in July.

Dollar buying was concentrated against EUR, JPY, CAD, NZD and, most notably, AUD, where the speculative net short surged to a fresh record of 182,000 contracts, equivalent to USD 12.3 billion. The Australian dollar remained under pressure following an unexpected decline in October employment, reinforcing expectations that the Reserve Bank of Australia has reached the end of its tightening cycle.

Overall, the data points to a renewed preference for dollar exposure even before the subsequent equity market turmoil intensified demand for liquidity and defensive positioning. With the reporting period ending on Tuesday, the full impact of the late-week selloff will not become visible until next week's report.

Gold final thoughts following another brutal day across markets. 

The dash for cash, dollar strength, the AI calamity and deeply negative momentum are powerful forces that, for now, are overriding just about everything else. We have broken price levels that few thought possible, leaving plenty of traders and investors nursing painful losses, made worse by the turmoil in equities. Simply put, this is not a great time for risk-taking, especially as we approach year-end, when the appetite for establishing fresh positions tends to fade.

The massive elephant in the room, besides growing pains in AI related stocks, remains inflation and what the Fed intends to do about it. My thinking is that we may see another rate hike, but not the series currently being priced in. Strip out the AI-driven investment boom, and the underlying US economy looks considerably less impressive. If that engine starts to sputter, as Nvidia, the self-appointed central bank of AI, continues to tumble, the FOMC may soon find itself singing a rather different tune. Note  Reuters reported an SEC probe into Nvidia exploring potential accounting issues.

We are not there yet, but with energy prices falling, particularly diesel, and the equity market increasingly showing signs of distress, I suspect the Fed may hesitate before pulling the trigger next month. Inflation remains the key, and any evidence that price pressures are easing could quickly challenge the market’s increasingly hawkish expectations.

In the meantime, gold’s best chance of a rebound may simply be that the selling has become excessive. Together with silver and platinum, the metal is looking increasingly oversold, raising the prospect of a technical bounce. Whether that develops into something more sustainable will depend on the dollar, yields and, above all, a shift in the prevailing risk-off sentiment.

For now, this is a time to keep a cool head and remember that we have been here many times before. Gold has a habit of testing even the most committed relationships. First comes disappointment, then falling out of love, followed by serious thoughts of divorce. But just when you are ready to walk away, the old sparkle has a funny way of returning.

Enjoy your weekend despite the bruises

Copper inventories: US stock concentration highlights potential shift towards China
Copper inventories monitored by the three major futures exchanges rose for a third consecutive week, increasing by 5,234 tonnes to 1.093 million tonnes. The modest overall build, however, masks a continued geographical imbalance, with US warehouses holding the overwhelming majority of exchange-monitored stocks.

LME inventories rose by 2,925 tonnes to 332,025, but this increase was entirely driven by an 8,550-tonne build at US warehouses to 249,200 tonnes. Excluding the US, LME inventories would have fallen by 5,625 tonnes, highlighting continued tightness elsewhere. Meanwhile, CME inventories recorded a second consecutive weekly decline, partly offsetting small increases in London and Shanghai.

Despite the recent reductions, CME warehouses still account for an elevated 67% of combined exchange inventories. Including copper held in LME-approved US warehouses lifts the US share to approximately 90%, underscoring the substantial concentration of available exchange stocks in a single market.

The concentration reflects the tariff-driven stockpiling of copper in the US over the past two years, but recent developments suggest these flows may now - but only partly - be starting to reverse. An acute shortage of deliverable copper in China has triggered a historic squeeze in nearby Shanghai futures, while the Yangshan import premium has surged to a record USD 500 per tonne. According to recent reports, traders have begun booking shipments of copper from the US to China, initially involving relatively modest volumes of tens of thousands of tonnes.

With the COMEX premium over LME copper having largely disappeared amid reduced expectations of US import tariffs, the incentive to keep metal in the US has weakened. A part reversal in trade flows could help ease China's physical supply squeeze while reducing the unusually large US inventory overhang. However, the timing and scale will depend on whether Chinese premiums remain sufficiently elevated to cover shipping costs and compensate traders for the risk of renewed US tariff measures.

Beyond higher yields and expectations of further Fed rate hikes hurting global growth prospects, the broad-based selloff may also reflect tightening global dollar liquidity. Rising AI-related financing needs, IPO activity, equity market volatility and elevated energy security costs are boosting demand for cash just as higher interest rates make funding more expensive.

Precious and industrial metals have borne the brunt of the rout, with the AI-driven equity selloff triggering double-digit weekly losses in silver and platinum, while copper has slumped 9.5% to an eight-month low. Gold, despite its safe-haven status, has also been caught in the broader dash for cash, falling 8% as investors liquidate highly liquid assets to meet funding needs, cover losses elsewhere and reduce overall risk exposure.

The energy sector is down 4% on the week, with Brent settling into a narrow range in the low USD 90s amid alternating focus on rising supply from the Middle East and the risk of flare-ups. From an inflation perspective, the more encouraging development has been the sharper decline in distillate fuel prices, with London gasoil down 8% on the week to USD 158 per barrel, compared with around USD 200 at the start of the month. Meanwhile, agriculture is down around 2.5%, weighed down primarily by the stronger dollar and broader risk aversion.
